title: Listen Like You’re Wrong
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author proposes that leaders start conversations presuming they may be wrong or missing something, which turns them from advocates into curious learners. Many seasoned leaders cannot do this because they are wedded to their views and listen only as a means to persuade. Listening like you are wrong shifts the stance from judging to engaging, with more questions than statements. He offers an exercise: list your facts, premises and biases, presume some are dead wrong, and then enter the conversation to understand the other person's perspective. His closing claim is that the intention to understand rather than reply defines true listening, and discomfort signals the need to try.
points: Presuming you may be wrong turns you from an advocate for your opinions into a curious learner.
Many seasoned leaders listen only to persuade, so they learn little from others.
The practice shifts from judging to engaging, favoring inquiry over advocacy.
A concrete exercise: identify your own premises and biases, presume some are dead wrong, then listen for the flaw.
The more uncomfortable the practice feels, the more important it is to attempt it.
quotes: Starting conversations with the premise that you are likely wrong in your thinking or understanding makes you a much different listener. Listening with the presumption that there is something you don’t know but need to is equally powerful. In both cases, you become less of an advocate for your opinions and more curious about what you can learn.

Listening to understand and fully grasp what others are saying is an acquired skill. For some seasoned leaders, it is an almost impossible skill to master because they are too wedded to their own views. They learn little from interacting with others, largely because that is not their goal. They remain committed advocates. They listen as a means to persuade.

Listening like you are wrong requires a shift in thinking from judging to engaging. You suspend the need to judge, at least temporarily, and engage others with the goal of understanding what premise or idea you have that might be faulty. Of course, this requires more questions than statements and more inquiry than advocacy.
Try this in an upcoming conversation. Clarify your views about the topic to be considered and identify the facts, premises, and biases you might have. Now presume one or more of them are dead wrong.

The intention to understand rather than reply is what constitutes true listening in the first place. In reality, leaders only hear what they understand. Listening like you’re wrong is a great step toward true understanding. Now see if you can do it. The more uncomfortable it makes you, the more critical it is for you to try.
